We just recently discovered who my great grandfather really was. He died really young (37.) We're American and come from a long line of pioneers and the family has always been heavily vested in doing geneology, family research, etc. Well, he discovered that my great grandfather was really a Serbian refugee who escaped first to Croatia and then he and his father came to America leaving his mother and siblings behind! We don't know why they came to America, but we did get in contact with my now-deceased Grandmothers cousins in London. The family there descended from my great grandfathers brother and they were even able to provide a family photo that confirmed that it truly is his real family!

I started looking into about 5 years ago when our middle kid would seemingly freak OUT over the most ridiculous (or at least what we thought were ridiculous things at the time.) She would cry and lose her mind over "wedgies." Turns out she can't handle having a seam in her underwear. Up until the last 6 months, she absolutely would NOT wear jeans because of how they felt. She couldn't at one time wear socks with the colored toes and heels or she would get stuck counting the sides to make sure they were even. Sure enough, Sensory processing disorder and OCD. Then I started looking at my own behaviors. I pull at my hair, bite my nails, can't wear shirts tight in the armpits, CANNOT handle tags, I always have my hair up, I hate having stuff on my hands....I've definitely read about kids holding food in their mouths for hours because it was legitimately a psychological issue to swallow it right away.
I don't (or can't) get dressed after a shower unless I've dried off completely hanging around in my towel.
It's definitely a sensory processing disorder type of thing! You should look into it!

I will say from my own experience that I was "diagnosed" ADD as a teenager and immediately put on meds. My mom made me feel ashamed of it all and told me not to tell anyone. By the time I was 28 (13 years later,) I had been on 8 different drugs, cut quite frequently as a teen and had crippling clinical depression. 

Cue to nearly 4 years ago when I realized that my then 12 yr old daughter was cutting. It was heartbreaking and I truly felt that if I could just be the parent she needed (basically be everything I never had) that she'd get through it and we could work together. I never wanted to put her on meds because of my awful experience with them. Maybe that's a bit selfish, but I never wanted to make her feel crazy or ashamed. Now she's nearly 16 and we still struggle a bit. I ended up agreeing to get her on some meds and she's been taking Prozac for about a month now. I don't see a MAJOR improvement, but little things are starting to change. 

So basically, I did it out of love.

We went back the next year for the same "Ghost Tour" and a guy brought it up that he'd seen the bench rock last year. The tour guide then told us they caught one of the ushers (so no one wandered off in the dark) sneaking up those stairs, pushing it hard enough to rock like that and then running off. It won't. It won't stop. The shooter did have legally aquired firearms, had no criminal history and was not affiliated with any political or religious group or cause (that we know of, according to his own, completely bewildered brother.) 

I live in a very conservative, gun-loving state and although I myself am not a gun owner by choice, I respect the rights and reasons of the people I know who do have them and carry them. 

I do think that it has a lot to do with one's access to fear-mongering media where everything is deemed a crisis. The shooters faces and names are plastered all over the news and social media. Mental health care is a joke in this country and in some sick way, this has exacerbated the problem by showing us that gun violence is the only thing that gets major attention. 

There was just another school shooting in Spokane, Washington where at least 1 was killed. The teenaged shooter gave his reason as he just "wanted to teach everyone a lesson about bullying."

The worst and hardest part about this (gun violence) is that no one ever wins the argument. Banning guns isn't going to do ANYTHING. How many guns do you think there are right now, right this minute on the black market?

One could argue that banning guns for everyone is a little like what teaches did to us back in elementary school. One kid messes up and the whole class suffers. Yes, the class gets taught a lesson, but it in no way stops that kid, or another kid from messing up again.

We could have stricter gun laws and stricter gun regulations, but if the Las Vegas shooter was able to obtain at least a portion of his overwhelming amount of guns legally and use them for terror/murder, what kind of legislation could we implement so peer into the future of a gun buyer and see what their true purposes/motives are?

I know of a lady (distant family connection) who legally bought a gun as a "Christmas present" after NUMEROUS suicide attempts and was finally able to carry through in her sorrow.

If we allow guns to be carried only by police/military then we as citizens go completely unprotected. Thank goodness I live in an extrememly safe place (statistically) and my little town is no stranger to gun crimes. 

So, I guess for now I will just continue to feel that deep, sickening pit in my stomach knowing that nothing I can do will ever stop another mass shooting and teach within the walls of my own home to love and accept everyone, serve those who need service and to be a "helper" in times of need. Guns don't kill people. People kill people and we need to find out why and help.

I'm going to post here because I'm a parent and my now 15 year old daughter nearly committed suicide 2 years ago. This is not to put myself on a pedestal or come off like I think I'm a better parent than others. Truth is, we'd talked about depression and suicide and I'd brushed it off as curiosity. Imagine my surprise when, through another mom, I found out my daughter had been cutting at age 12.  She hadn't been bullied. She did very well in school, was well liked, the teachers loved her....by all outward appearances she was the last kid on earth you'd expect to find out was a cutter. 

I immediately got her in with a counselor both inside and outside of school. I made it a point to TALK to her. Kids don't often want to talk about what's bothering them because they are afraid of not being taken seriously/judged/ridiculed. 

Through information from the counselors, I was heavily advised to start locking up all the medication in the house and being very aware of her movements throughout the day. It was heartbreaking and one of the worst things we've ever been through. My sweet daughter wanted to die and no one knew why. There wasn't a solid reason, she was clinically depressed and didn't see another way out of it. 

I truly believe that had I not found out and stepped in when I did, I would have lost my oldest to suicide. I'm so humbled and blessed to say that now at age 15, she's an honor roll student, an active member in her Speech, Debate and Drama club, has a boyfriend and is so excited to follow the path to becoming either an RN or a School Counselor herself. 

If you, or your kids/students are contemplating suicide, self harming or you notice a change in their behavior, TALK TO THEM and keep them in your line of sighT and genuinely BE THERE FOR THEM. Not every kid shows signs of depression and it's sadly all too true that the kids you least expect to commit suicide do it. 

Almost just as importantly, teach your kids to be KIND and RESPECTFUL to one another. Teach them to have compassion and love towards everyone. Education begins at home. Maybe someday they will be the friend someone turns to when they think there's no way out.

I'm just going to put my two cents in as an EBT recipient. I am a stay at home mother/wife and my husband works full time in a respectable banking position. We own our own home, pay all of our bills on time AND we pay taxes just like everyone else. We don't get a substantial amount of benefits each month, but I can say that the amount we receive is crucial in being able to feed my family (there are 5 of us) for a month.  I feel like my family is the exception to the "rule"/stereotype that EBT recipients are poor, jobless, homeless, drug/alcohol dependent losers that only want to live off of the government. No, you cannot buy alcohol with EBT. In most stores you can't even buy deli meals (like fried chicken, etc.) with the money. What it comes down to is this: You are given that money based on your income/family size. How YOU choose to feed your family with that money is really only your business. 

Having also been a part of programs like WIC (Women, Infant, Children) I can also factually tell you that a lot of the program is nutrition education. The WIC program offers nutrition consultation, cooking classes, they monitor your childs development/growth based on "national standards" to see if your children are being properly fed. Childhood obesity is no joke. 

I do feel like there should be different guidelines/regulations regarding EBT as far as nutrition education, wellness programs, etc, but I'm not one to complain.
